forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bassetlaw's forecast moves from £2.231m surplus to £2.769m cumulative gap by March 2030
news_drafts.lead:
Bassetlaw District Council's Cabinet has been given an updated medium-term financial plan (MTFP, the council's forecast of spending against income over the next few years) showing a cumulative budget gap of £2.769m by March 2030. In February 2026 the same forecast showed a cumulative surplus of £2.231m through to March 2029, a swing of about £5m.

The council attributes the change to updated funding assumptions, confirmed after the government's three-year Local Government Finance Settlement. The papers do not break the £5m down further.

The council plans to manage the gap in three ways. It will draw on earmarked reserves (money set aside for a named purpose): £1.650m in 2026/27, then £481,000 and £1.161m in the following two years. It will identify further savings and efficiency measures through future budget processes, though the papers do not put a figure on these. And it expects some help from the outcome of future government Spending Reviews. For 2029/30 the plan is to use the Financial Resilience Reserve, set up for this purpose, alongside additional savings. The council says relying on reserves to balance the budget carries inherent risks and is not sustainable in the long term.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £2.769m by March 2030 to be closed through reserves, unidentified future savings, and spending review outcomes
findings.detail: Council strategy combines three approaches: planned drawdown of earmarked reserves to smooth deficit (£1.650m in 2026/27, then £481k and £1.161m in following years); identification of further savings and efficiency measures through future budget processes (specific amount not yet quantified); and positive outcomes from future Government Spending Reviews. For 2029/30, plan is to use Financial Resilience Reserve established specifically for this purpose alongside additional savings. Council explicitly acknowledges that relying on reserves to balance budget carries inherent risks and is not sustainable long-term, indicating awareness that structural solutions (permanent savings) are required.
findings.matters: Shows both strength (deliberate reserve use as bridge to allow transformation time) and risk (relies on unidentified savings and positive spending review outcomes). Peers and lenders need to track whether promised savings emerge in future budget iterations and whether spending review assumptions prove realistic.
findings.figures: Cumulative gap £2.769m by 2029/30; 2026/27 reserve transfer £1.650m; annual transfers 2027/28-2028/29 of £481k and £1.161m
findings.quote: The forecast identifies a cumulative budget gap of £2.769m by 2029/30. This is expected to be managed through a combination of the earmarked reserves, the delivery of further savings and efficiency measures to be identified through future budget processes, and the outcome of future Spending Review settlements and government funding allocations.

findings.headline: CIPFA Financial Resilience Index shows marked improvement; capital gearing 30% below sector average of 37%
findings.detail: Despite emerging budget deficit, underlying financial health metrics improved. CIPFA Financial Resilience Index for 2024/25 shows marked improvement with stress indicators moving toward lower risk across most metrics over two years. Capital gearing decreased to 30% compared with HRA district average of 37%. LG Improve described council's position in assets and reserves as sound and resilient. These metrics suggest underlying financial position improving and more resilient than suggested by the emerging budget gap alone.
findings.matters: Supporting evidence that the council is managing financial pressures effectively. Underlying resilience improving even as temporary funding items expire suggests capacity and discipline to address identified budget gap through structural measures (savings and efficiencies) rather than through degradation of financial health.
findings.figures: Capital gearing 30% (HRA district average 37%); CIPFA metrics moved toward lower risk
findings.quote: There has been a marked improvement in the CIPFA Financial Index in 2024/25 (the latest available data) with a movement in financial stress indicators towards 'lower risk' across most indicators over the last two years.

findings.headline: Revenue dependency on council tax at 72.4%, forecast to rise further, constrained by 2.99% government referendum threshold
findings.detail: Council tax comprises 72.4% of revenue (2024/25), forecast rising further. This concentration is significantly above comparable councils and creates multiple income vulnerabilities. Government limits annual increases to 2.99% through referendum threshold. Should Local Government Reorganisation proceed, council tax harmonisation could affect income: the council notes it currently has one of the higher district-level charges in Nottinghamshire. Growth depends on housing delivery per Local Plan. The council tax reduction scheme also reduces tax base for lower-income residents.
findings.matters: High council tax dependency creates specific vulnerabilities that peer councils and lenders monitor closely. The combination of government referendum caps, potential harmonisation risk from LGR, and reliance on housing growth creates multiple income pressure points beyond council's direct control.
findings.figures: Council tax 72.4% of 2024/25 revenue; government referendum threshold 2.99% per annum; council tax base growth 1.4% from 2027/28
findings.quote: The index highlights Bassetlaw's reliance on council tax as a substantial portion of its revenue (2025/26: 72.4%)

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collections tracking ahead of budget targets despite cost-of-living pressures
findings.detail: At end of Q1 2026/27, council tax collection reached 24.65% of expected annual yield against profiled target of 24.25%, and business rates achieved 28.33% against target of 24.75%. Overall collection rate stands at 94.7% (down marginally from 95.2% the prior year but still robust). This performance is significant given broader economic uncertainty and cost-of-living pressures affecting residents and businesses.
findings.matters: Tax collection rate is a leading indicator of income stability and underlying economic conditions. Strong performance mitigates some vulnerability created by heavy council tax dependence (72.4% of revenue), and provides evidence that household and business tax bases are resilient to current economic conditions.
findings.figures: Council Tax collection 24.65% (target 24.25%); Business Rates 28.33% (target 24.75%); collection rate 94.7%
findings.quote: At the end of Quarter 1, the Council had collected 24.65% of Council Tax, exceeding the profiled target of 24.25%. Business Rates collection performance was similarly positive, achieving 28.33% against a target of 24.75%.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves increased £3.509m in 2025/26, ranked 4th for movement among 64 comparable councils
findings.detail: Despite emerging budget deficit, the council's financial resilience strengthened materially in 2025/26. General Fund useable reserves increased by £3.509m: general reserves rose to £4.137m (from £3.011m) and earmarked reserves rose to £13.470m (from £11.088m). LG Improve ranked the council 4th out of 64 HRA district councils for pace of reserve building, suggesting deliberate reserve building to address known future pressures rather than reactive management.
findings.matters: The reserve building trajectory shows a council actively building financial buffers against a forecast deficit, rather than being forced to raid reserves to meet current obligations. The pace of building (4th among peers) suggests financial discipline and forward planning capability.
findings.figures: Reserves increase £3.509m; General Fund balance £5.137m (from £4.011m); earmarked reserves £13.470m (from £11.088m); 4th out of 64 councils
findings.quote: The Council's useable GF revenue reserves have increased by £3.509m during the year • General reserves £4.137m (£3.011m as of 31st March 2026) • Earmarked reserves £13.470m (£11.088m as of 31st March 2026)

daily_post.headline: Salary costs forecast £235,120 against budget £210,000, a £25,120 overrun that accounts for the entire profit swing
daily_post.lead: Salary costs are controllable expenditure; an unbudgeted 12% increase signals either unplanned headcount growth or unbudgeted pay awards, both material to forecast reliability and the entity's financial management
